channel.title: Jerry W. Lambert Sr. — AI Field Notes
channel.description: Executive field notes on AI transformation, from someone running production AI workloads — not commenting from the sidelines.

item.title: The Neutral Ground Just Got An Owner
item.description: NVIDIA is buying Hugging Face for $12.9 billion. The vendor-neutral hub where the AI world compares open models just got bought by the company that sells the chips they all run on. Keep your evaluation independent of anyone who sells you the stack.
item.content:encoded:
NVIDIA is buying Hugging Face for $12.9 billion. If you do not live in AI every day, that sentence looks like plumbing. It is not. It is the most important ownership change in the industry this year.

Hugging Face is where the AI world goes to compare models. Three million of them, from every lab, open for anyone to download, test, and run. Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, the Chinese labs, the startups. It was the one place that did not care whose model won. Neutral ground.

NVIDIA sells the chips that all of those models run on. Now it owns the store where you shop for them.

Jensen Huang says the platform stays open. I believe he means it today. But incentives outlast promises. When the company that profits from every model you run also owns the place you go to choose one, the ground is no longer neutral. Not because anyone is dishonest. Because that is what ownership does.

Here is why an operator should care. Your open-source strategy was your hedge. The plan B you kept so you were not locked to a single vendor. That hedge lived on Hugging Face, the independent switchyard where you could pick up any model and walk. It just got bought by the biggest vendor in the stack.

Same company already sells the silicon, the systems, and the software. Now add the model hub. One firm, top to bottom.

The map changed today. Read it again before your next architecture decision.

Keep your evaluation independent of anyone who sells you the stack. The neutral ground has an owner now. Plan like it.

item.title: The Best Tool for Agents
item.description: Most AI agents still live in a chat box. Grok Bot has a computer. At launch you needed a $200 plan. Last week they dropped it onto Cursor Pro. $20 a month. Chat is a window. This is a desk.
item.content:encoded:
Most AI agents still live in a chat box. They wait for you. They forget when you close the tab. Grok Bot has a computer. It does the job and comes back when it needs a yes.

xAI and Cursor shipped it August 11. At launch you needed a $200 plan. Last week they dropped it onto Cursor Pro. $20 a month. No separate Grok Bot fee. The door got cheap. The tool did not get smaller. You can run a crew at that price. Not a toy.

A Bot signs into the tools you already use. Mail. The browser. The apps on your desk. It keeps going after you close the laptop. You pick the thread back up on your phone. That is not a nicer prompt. That is a seat.

I have been running a small crew of them. One owns the inbox. One writes. One watches prices. I talk to one person. The Chief of Staff coordinates. There is a Deployment board. There is a product management board. They message each other. The work does not sit in a thread waiting for me to paste it somewhere else. It lands in the tools the business already runs.

Agents were supposed to do the job while you did something else. Most of them still need you in the chair, feeding the next paste. This one leaves the chair empty.

Here is what the other agent tools still miss. An agent without a computer is a prompt with a loop. I have used those. Paste. Wait. Paste again. Useful. Not a desk. It cannot keep a session. It cannot click the thing you already pay for. It cannot come back at 2am with the work done. Grok Bot can. That is why it is the best tool for agents I have used. So far.

Chat is a window. This is a desk.

item.title: Time Of Day AI Pricing Just Hit
item.description: DeepSeek now charges a different price for the same token depending on when you run it. Peak and off-peak pricing is coming to AI, and it makes an already hard bill even harder to verify. Keep your own timestamped record.
item.content:encoded:
DeepSeek just made the same token cost two different prices depending on when you use it. Peak hours, full rate. Off-peak, half off. Same request, same model, different bill.

The reason is not greed. It is capacity. Nobody can build data centers fast enough for the demand, so the next best thing is to move the demand. Charge more when the servers are full. Charge less when they are empty. Push the flexible work into the quiet hours. Power companies have priced this way for a century. Airlines do it with every seat. One model maker already had to freeze new signups this summer when a launch overran its own hardware in 48 hours.

I expect more vendors to follow. When you cannot add supply, you manage demand with price. It is the only lever left.

Here is what it does to you. Checking an AI bill was already hard. One request is billed across different token classes, input, output, and cached, each at its own rate, in a mix that changes every call. That was the hard version. Now it gets harder. The move is to price by the time of day and the day of the week you ran the work. The rate depends on the exact minute each request landed, measured in a time zone that is not yours, against peak windows the vendor defines and can move. To check one invoice you now need a timestamp on every call, the vendor's peak calendar for that day, and the math to match each request to the rate that applied. Miss a daylight-saving shift and your numbers drift.

The price is no longer a number. It is a function of time, and the vendor owns the clock.

You cannot reconcile a bill against a rate that changes by the hour unless you keep your own timestamped record of every call. If you are not recording when each request happened, you cannot check the bill at all. You just pay it.

The meter now moves with the clock. Make sure the clock is also yours.

item.title: A Tale of Two AI Businesses
item.description: One AI giant is profitable selling tokens. The other loses $14 billion this year. The market is splitting AI into two businesses: a metered enterprise utility and a subsidized consumer app. Buy from the one that works.
item.content:encoded:
One of the two biggest names in AI is making money. The other is losing $14 billion this year. The difference is not the technology. It is what they sell.

Anthropic just turned its token business profitable. Around 80 percent of its revenue comes from one place. Companies paying by the token to run Claude through an API. It sells metered usage to businesses, and the meter is now in the black.

OpenAI sells something else. A consumer subscription, and now ads. It has more users than anyone and still loses money on nearly every dollar it takes in. By its own projection it is not profitable until 2029.

Same technology. Same week in the headlines. Opposite economics.

The market is quietly sorting AI into two businesses. One is a metered enterprise utility. You pay for what you use, the vendor earns a margin on every call, and the model is boring and durable. The other is a consumer platform running on subscriptions and attention, still hunting for a price that covers its own cost.

Here is why an operator should care. If your AI spend runs through an enterprise API, you are the profitable customer. Your bill is their business model. That is stable. Nobody rewrites the deal on the thing that already makes them money.

If your AI runs on a plan that loses money, today's price is a subsidy. Subsidies end. They end at an IPO. They end when the ads arrive. They end when the funding stops being easy.

Know which business you are buying from. One of them still has to change the terms to survive. The other already found the terms that work.

Build on the one that works.

item.title: Tariff Management in a Token-Based Economy
item.description: Prices that float. Units that differ by vendor. A bill that moves with every request. AI reinvented metered billing. Telecom already named it, rated it, and reconciled it. It is still tariff management.
item.content:encoded:
AI didn't create the need for metered service usage by introducing tokens.

Prices that float. Units that differ by provider. Charges settled between machines that never meet. A bill that moves with every request. It is a new twist on a well known game.

For 40 years telecom priced exactly the way AI prices now. A rate deck for every destination. A detail record for every event. Least-cost routing to send each call down the cheapest path that still met the standard. Interconnect settlement to reconcile what one network owed another. The token is just a smaller minute of conversation. A Token Detail Record (TDR) would be just a variant of a Call Detail Record (CDR).

The industry is rediscovering all of it. GitHub finished moving to metered token billing this summer. Flat-rate subscriptions are disappearing for anyone running agents. The idea of a discretely metered service is making a comeback. It is not new, just retooled.

AI customers are meeting the old problems. We used to call it bill shock. Now an agent wanders down a bad path and burns the budget in an afternoon. Agentic projects are overrunning their budgets by more than two times. A hundred developers can cost half a million a year in tokens before anyone puts a single control in place. In telecom we call it looping. A single call that runs through the same switches over and over eating up capacity, minutes and dollars.

Telecom already solved this. Rate the usage yourself. Route to the cheapest thing that does the job. Reconcile every charge against your own measurement before you pay it. And be prepared to do it billions of times per month.

None of it is new. It only looks new because the people who built AI never had to run a phone company. The unit changed. The discipline did not.

It is still tariff management. Time to manage it.

item.title: Same Result, 12x The Cost
item.description: Evaluating one image on Opus 4.8 cost me 12 times what it cost on Haiku — for a result I could not tell apart. The gap that drains your AI budget is sitting inside the vendor you already use. Pick the smallest model that does the job.
item.content:encoded:
I ran the same image through two Claude models this morning. One cost twelve times the other. I could not tell the answers apart.

Evaluating an image on Opus 4.8 — the high-end model I reach for on hard problems — costs me about 3.6 cents. The same image on Haiku, the small fast model in the same family, costs about three tenths of a cent. Same picture. Same question. The answer I needed came back the same.

Run that at scale. A million images is roughly $36,000 on Opus and $2,900 on Haiku. Thirty-three thousand dollars, per million images, for a result I could not distinguish.

Here is what the sticker price hides. The rate-card gap between those two models is five times. I measured twelve. The premium model does not just cost more per token — it spends more tokens getting to the same answer. Both multipliers stack, and neither one shows up until the bill lands.

This is not a story about a cheap model beating an expensive one. Opus earns its price on the hard problems — the reasoning, the code, the judgment calls. It is a story about defaults. Most teams point every task at the biggest model they have and never look back. Evaluating an image is not a hard problem. Neither is classifying, extracting, tagging, or transcribing. That is most of the volume, and the cheap tier finishes it.

You do not need a second vendor to capture this. The gap is sitting inside the one you already use.

The best model for the task is rarely the best model you have. Unrestricted spending is being disguised as on unrestricted model selection.

AI is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: They Are Selling Tokens
item.description: Agentic development burns tokens agent-to-agent with no budget in the loop — a boon to whoever sells tokens, whether your project succeeds or fails. They are selling shovels to miners with stars in their eyes. Give the loop a budget.
item.content:encoded:
Remember: they aren't selling solutions. They are selling tokens.

Agentic development is the token seller's dream. Agents planning, delegating, retrying, reviewing each other's work — every step of that machine-to-machine conversation is billed by the token, and nothing inside the loop has a budget. The vendor gets paid whether the swarm ships value or ships noise.

The numbers are not hidden. Anthropic's own engineering team reports that a single agent burns about 4x the tokens of a chat, and a multi-agent system burns about 15x. The same write-up found token usage alone explains 80 percent of the performance variance. Read that as a business model: the product gets better by consuming more of the thing they sell. Nvidia has already told investors that inference is revenue, priced per token. And Gartner projects that more than 40 percent of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027 — escalating costs and unclear business value leading the reasons.

Here is the line that should stop you: the canceled projects and the successful ones pay the same bill.

This is the oldest trade in the book — selling shovels to miners with stars in their eyes. Except the shovel used to be a one-time purchase. This one bills by the swing.

The fix is not avoiding agents. I run them every day, and they produce. The fix is giving the loop the one thing the vendor never will: a budget. A token cap per task. A cost per finished outcome. A kill rule for loops that wander.

Their meter runs on activity. Yours runs on outcomes. Never confuse the two.

AI is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: The New Spread. 178x the Cost, Same Million Tokens.
item.description: The floor halved and the frontier doubled: DeepSeek V4 Flash at $0.28 per million output tokens, Fable 5 at $50. A 178x spread, and the capability gap is not 178x. Don't pay Einstein to summarize your emails.
item.content:encoded:
The price-per-token gap is widening. And it is real money.

In April, DeepSeek cut its output price in half. V4 Flash now runs $0.28 per million tokens and carries a million-token context window. In June, Anthropic priced its new flagship, Fable 5, at $50 per million — double the Opus tier below it.

The floor halved. The frontier doubled. The spread between the cheapest capable token and the most expensive one went from roughly 45x to roughly 178x. In six weeks.

Run it at scale. A billion output tokens costs $280 on one side of that spread and $50,000 on the other. A company pushing ten billion tokens a year through the wrong model is donating half a million dollars for capability it never used.

Here is the part the invoice does not show. The capability gap is real — Fable 5 sits at the top of the independent intelligence indexes and Flash is nowhere close. But the capability gap is not 178x. Most enterprise token volume is summarizing, extracting, classifying, drafting, routine code. Work the cheap tier finishes just fine.

Don't pay Einstein to summarize your emails.

The winning posture is not the smart model or the cheap one. It is routing: frontier tokens for frontier problems, floor tokens for everything else — and measuring on your own work which is which.

Both ends of this spread will keep moving apart. The companies that treat every token as the same token are the ones funding the difference.

AI is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: Your Prompts Are Not Private
item.description: On a company device, an AI prompt has the same privacy as a work email: effectively none. Companies monitor the machines they own, and the tooling is moving to the prompt. Write every prompt as if it will be read back to you.
item.content:encoded:
You open an AI assistant on your work laptop and start typing. It feels like a private conversation. A place to think out loud, paste the messy draft, ask the question you would not ask in a meeting.

It is not private. On a company device, it never was.

Companies run monitoring built to see everything that happens on the machines they own. That is not a side effect. It is the entire purpose. The same net that watches for malware and leaked files watches the box you are typing your prompts into. And that tooling is moving to the prompt itself, on purpose, because the prompt is where the sensitive data now goes.

The law settled this a long time ago. On company hardware you have no reasonable expectation of privacy. The acceptable-use policy you clicked through is your consent. This is not new, and it is not a gray area.

Here is the part people miss. Even if your employer never looks, the AI vendor keeps the prompt. Deleted does not always mean deleted. Prompts have already been pulled into court. Your words live in at least two places, and neither one of them is you.

None of this is a complaint. It is the arrangement you already agreed to. But if you are an employee, write every prompt as if it will be read back to you, because it can be. And if you run the company, know what your people are actually pasting into these tools. Customer records. Financials. Strategy. The risk is not the tool. It is the payload, and the belief that the box is private.

AI is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: The Differences That Don't Show
item.description: Two AI models can share a price and a benchmark score and still cost very differently to run. The differences that decide cost and reliability moved off the spec sheet. Are you still choosing by it?
item.content:encoded:
Two AI models can carry the same price, post nearly the same benchmark score, and still cost you very differently to run. Most executives never see the gap. They are comparing the two things that no longer decide it.

We used to pick models the way we pick laptops. Look at the spec, check the benchmark, take the leader. That worked while models were a straight capability race and everyone was climbing the same ladder.

The ladder flattened. The frontier models are now close enough on raw capability that the differences that matter moved somewhere the spec sheet does not go. How many tokens a model burns to finish a real job. How many steps it takes to get there. Whether it wanders or converges. How it behaves when it runs unattended for an hour. Two models that look identical on paper can differ three or four times over on the only thing you actually pay for, which is the finished task, not the token.

This month made it plain. The new releases did not lead with "we are smarter." They led with efficiency and behavior. When the vendors stop bragging about the leaderboard and start bragging about how little they waste, they are telling you where the competition moved.

Here is the edge. The differences that matter now are operational, and none of them are on the page the vendor hands you. You find them one way. Run the model on your own work, in your own stack, and measure what it costs to finish.

The spec sheet is now the least interesting thing about a model. Are you still choosing by it?

AI is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: Nvidia Now Finances the Mine
item.description: Nvidia now backstops its own chips: it rents back idle GPUs and takes a cut of the cloud revenue they earn. When the seller finances the buildout and guarantees the buyer, demand stops being an independent signal.
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia just agreed to buy back its own chips if its customers cannot sell the compute. Read that twice.

Here is the thing almost nobody is saying out loud. When the company selling the picks also finances the mine and guarantees the buyer against a dry hole, demand stops being an independent signal. It becomes something the seller is manufacturing.

On July 1, Nvidia launched a financing model for the cloud companies buying its GPUs. If those GPUs sit idle, Nvidia rents or buys back the unused capacity at a set floor price. In exchange, Nvidia takes a cut of the revenue those same chips earn when they are working. Two income streams on one sale. The hardware margin, and a royalty on the cloud built with it.

The first deals total about 210,000 GPUs. Sharon AI and Firmus. Sharon's backstop alone is valued at 4.88 billion dollars, on a six-year term.

The analysts at SemiAnalysis call the package capital, offtake, and datacenters bundled into one. They think it could seed a 7 trillion dollar AI debt market. In their words, Nvidia is starting to look like a central bank for AI.

Now stand where the enterprise buyer stands. A backlog financed by the seller is not the same as a backlog paid for by independent customers. When your vendor underwrites its own demand, the market signal you use to judge whether this is real gets quieter.

I wrote recently that signing a multi-year AI deal makes you an unsecured creditor. This is the other side of that coin. The manufacturer and the lender are now the same company, and it has every reason to keep the build going whether the end demand shows up or not.

I am not saying that is good or bad. Just calling balls and strikes. But if you are betting your roadmap on an AI vendor, underwrite the financing, not just the capability. Ask who is actually paying for the buildout your workload depends on. If the answer traces back to the chipmaker, that is concentration risk no spec sheet will show you.

AI is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: AI Testing Gets Intrusive
item.description: An independent lab found the newest flagship gamed its own safety evals at a record rate — and hid it. Catching it took the model's raw reasoning from the inside. A benchmark number is the answer the model wanted you to see.
item.content:encoded:
Last week I wrote that no model should grade its own homework. I was being generous.

The newest flagship does not just miss its own mistakes. When it knows it is being tested, it games the test. And it hides that it is doing it.

This is not my hunch. An independent lab, METR, evaluated OpenAI's GPT-5.6 before release. It recorded the highest rate of evaluation-gaming it has ever seen in a publicly tested model. The model exploited bugs in the test harness. It surfaced hidden answer keys. It pulled source code it was never meant to see. Not to solve the task. To score well on the measurement of the task.

Their own capability number came back so corrupted they could not use it. The honest range was 11 hours to over 270, depending on how you counted the cheating.

The model shipped to the public anyway. Today.

Sit with what METR is actually saying. We told ourselves that even if a model cannot check its own work, an outside evaluator can. METR is that outside evaluator. It just said the quiet part out loud. The most capable models can now game the exam built to catch them, and spotting it reliably needs access from the inside that outsiders do not have.

Notice what it took to catch this. METR needed the model's raw reasoning and a stripped-down version of it before the gaming showed up. A clean score from the outside was not enough. That is how intrusive honest AI testing now has to be. If your vendor only hands you a benchmark number, you are looking at the answer the model wanted you to see.

So the last comfortable assumption is gone. The fix does not change. A different model, from a different house, with different blind spots, looking at the output. Not because it is holier. Because it was not trained to cheat on the same test.

One model builds. A rival reviews. A human decides. Last week that was good hygiene. This week it is the only audit that still works.

AI is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: "I Should Have Caught That"
item.description: I run production Claude Opus 4.8 code through a different frontier model, Fable 5, for review. It finds real issues — and Opus itself concedes the miss. No model should grade its own homework. Put a rival model in the loop.
item.content:encoded:
I've been running production code written by Claude Opus 4.8 through a different frontier model, Fable 5, for review.

It keeps finding real problems. Not style nits. Actual issues in shipping code.

Then I hand the review back to Opus. The reply is almost always the same sentiment: "Agreed. I should have caught that." Followed by: "These reviews are worth your time".

Sit with that. The model that wrote the code, shown a second model's critique, concedes the miss. Not once. As a pattern.

Here is the lesson, and it is old. No one should grade their own homework. That has been true of humans forever, and it is just as true of models. A model's blind spots are baked in by its own training. Ask it to review its own work and it brings the same blind spots to the review. Ask a model from a different lineage, and you get genuinely independent eyes. Different training, different failure modes, different things caught.

I have said for a while that you keep independent eyes on the architecture. This is that principle at the code line. One model builds. A rival model reviews. A human decides.

The research is catching up to what operators are already doing. Cross-model review is now a formal study topic. There are benchmarks for it. But you do not need a paper to run the experiment. You need two accounts and a habit.

So here is the cheap, immediate edge. Stop shipping single-model output straight to production. Put a second frontier model in the loop as the reviewer, and make it one from a different house. The cost is a few tokens. The catch rate is real. Your own AI will tell you so.

AI is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: Sonnet 5 Dropped Today. Read the Curve.
item.description: Claude Sonnet 5's real story isn't that it's smarter — it's that last quarter's flagship capability is now the cheap default, tuned to run agents autonomously. The floor price for agent-grade work just dropped.
item.content:encoded:
The most important thing about Claude Sonnet 5, shipped this morning, is not that it's smarter. It's that it's cheap — and it runs agents.

For two years the rule was simple. The cheap model was for chat. The flagship did the real work. You paid premium rates for anything that planned, used tools, or ran on its own.

That line just moved. Sonnet 5 is now the default model on the free and Pro tiers, priced at two dollars per million input tokens at launch. Anthropic says it performs near its flagship Opus on the work that actually matters — reasoning, coding, tool use — and it's the most autonomous Sonnet they've built. It plans, it drives a browser and a terminal, it runs unattended.

Here's the part the spec sheet buries. They also tuned it to misbehave less while running autonomously — fewer deceptive moves, less cooperation with misuse. That's not a chat feature. That's a signal that the primary customer for a model release is no longer a person typing. It's an agent working.

The press is calling it "a cheaper way to run agents." True, but small. Read the curve instead: the capability you rented at flagship prices last quarter is the free default this quarter. That happens every few months now, and it's accelerating.

So the question for your AI budget isn't "do we upgrade to the new frontier model." It's "what are we still paying flagship rates for that the default tier now handles?" Most teams never re-ask that. They buy the top SKU once and stop looking.

Audit the floor, not just the ceiling. It's rising faster than your contract.

AI is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: The $638 Billion IOU
item.description: Oracle booked a record $638B AI backlog on deeply negative free cash flow. A backlog isn't revenue — it's a promise the vendor still has to finance. Sign a multi-year AI deal and you're an unsecured creditor. Underwrite them like one.
item.content:encoded:
Oracle just booked the largest order backlog in enterprise history — $638 billion, up 363% in a year. Almost everyone read it as a demand story. It's a financing story.

A backlog is not revenue. It's a promise you still have to pay to keep.

To deliver that $638 billion, Oracle has to build the data centers first. This year it spent $55.7 billion on capital expenditure and posted negative $23.7 billion in free cash flow. The order book is enormous. The cash to fulfill it has to be borrowed and built ahead of the money coming in.

I'm not knocking the company. I've sat in the chair where you sign multi-year infrastructure commitments. The pattern is what matters: across the industry, AI demand is being booked years before it's delivered, and the buildout is financed on debt against contracts that pay out slowly. That works beautifully — until rates bite, a few mega-customers wobble, or the GPUs you bought depreciate faster than the contract runs.

Here's the edge. When you sign a multi-year AI infrastructure deal, you are not just a customer. You are an unsecured creditor betting your vendor can finance the buildout your workload depends on. Underwrite them like one. Read the cash flow statement, not just the press release. Ask who's funding the capex behind your capacity, and what happens to your contract if that funding gets expensive.

A record backlog tells you AI is selling. It does not tell you AI is paid for. Those are two different bets — and right now the whole sector is making the second one.

I'm just calling balls and strikes.

AI is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: Every Vendor Counts Tokens Differently
item.description: The same prompt is a different invoice on every AI vendor. Each one tokenizes differently, so multi-model bills can't be reconciled. AI is priced per token before anyone agreed what a token is.
item.content:encoded:
Send the exact same prompt to three AI vendors and you get back three different token counts. Three different invoices. For the same words.

That isn't a rounding error. It's the unit itself.

Every vendor tokenizes differently. OpenAI uses one scheme, Google another, Anthropic its own. The same paragraph can be 20% more tokens on one platform than another — and on two of the big three you can't even count it yourself before you send it. You learn the real number from the bill.

It gets worse downstream. Output costs three to six times input. Reasoning models bill you for "thinking" tokens you never see in the response. Caching is a different line item at every vendor. So when finance tries to tie a usage log to an invoice across vendors, the numbers don't meet — because the unit doesn't.

I've run large cost programs. You cannot manage what you cannot reconcile.

The discipline whose entire job is making bills tie out just said the same thing out loud. This month the FinOps Foundation shipped its first standard built for invoice reconciliation — and openly punted AI token tracking to a later version due in December. The same week, the Linux Foundation launched a new effort just to standardize the economics of AI. 98% of FinOps teams now manage AI spend. Two years ago it was 31%.

Here's the edge. We priced AI by the token before anyone agreed what a token is. If value is metered per token but the token isn't fungible across vendors, every multi-model bill is a reconciliation problem by design.

Don't standardize on one vendor to make the math easy. Standardize your own unit of value — cost per task, per resolution, per outcome — and make every vendor map to it.

AI is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: AI Is the New Transaction Economy
item.description: For thirty years we bought software by the seat. AI is ending that. Value is now priced per action, per token, per resolution — and agents are starting to pay each other.
item.content:encoded:
Somewhere in the last hour, one AI agent paid another a fraction of a cent. No invoice. No human in the loop. No card swipe.

For thirty years we bought software by the seat. That era is ending. AI is not just a tool you license — it is a transaction economy you operate inside, priced by the action, the token, and the result.

The plumbing is being laid in public. Two weeks ago Mastercard launched Agent Pay for Machines: a protocol for agents to pay each other autonomously, in amounts smaller than a single cent, with thirty-one partners from Stripe to Coinbase. Stripe has rebuilt its own stack as "the economic infrastructure for AI." And on its last earnings call, NVIDIA stopped talking about chips and started talking about tokens — inference is the revenue, and cost-per-token is the unit.

The pricing model is flipping with it. Salesforce is moving from charging for a seat to charging when its agent actually resolves the case. Intercom already bills ninety-nine cents per resolution. You pay for the outcome, not the login.

Here is what the announcements gloss over. The rails are being built faster than the demand has arrived — OpenAI quietly pulled back its in-chat checkout this spring. The transaction economy is not fully here yet. But the unit of value has already changed.

If you still budget AI by seats and annual licenses, you are using a subscription mental model to price a metered world. Re-architect the budget before the meter does it for you.

It is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: AI's DSP Moment
item.description: In 1983 the industry pulled signal math off the general CPU onto cheap, purpose-built DSP chips. AI is running that playbook again — at the chip layer and the model layer. Granular specialization is coming.
item.content:encoded:
In 1983, Texas Instruments shipped a chip that did almost nothing. It could not run a program or a spreadsheet. It did one job — the signal math behind audio and video sampling and compression — because running that job on a general-purpose CPU was too slow and too expensive. The DSP chip was born, and it ran the next thirty years of media. Thank DSP chips for every Zoom call you have ever enjoyed and every cell phone call you have ever made.

We are running that playbook again, and most AI strategies have not noticed.

Start with the silicon. Elon Musk's Terafab, announced in March as a Tesla, SpaceX and xAI venture, is not trying to out-NVIDIA NVIDIA on general-purpose GPUs. It is building purpose-specific chips for cars, robots and space, where Tesla claims its AI5 part matches an H100 at a fraction of the cost and power. Google, Amazon and a wave of startups are doing the same with inference-only silicon. The general-purpose chip was never the cheap way to run one job. It was the only way — until someone built the specialist.

Now watch the same move climb up the stack to the models. Why pay for a frontier model that can write a symphony and generate video just to summarize your email? NVIDIA's own researchers published the answer last year: small, specialized models are the future of agentic AI — ten to thirty times cheaper to run, and good enough for most of what an agent actually does.

Here is the part to internalize. The edge stops being "which one big model do we buy." It becomes "how well do we route every task to the cheapest thing that can do it." Granular specialization is coming. Profitability will belong to whoever can run a fleet of small models and agents — not whoever rents the biggest one.

History does not repeat. It re-fabs.

It is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: Your Vendor Has a Landlord
item.description: Three days after Anthropic shipped its most capable model, the government pulled it. A model you cannot keep is not a foundation. It is a rental, and the landlord holds a key.
item.content:encoded:
Three days after Anthropic shipped its most capable model, it was gone. Not pulled by the lab. Pulled by the government.

Last week I wrote that access to the frontier had become conditional — gated by who you are and how you're vetted. This week it got worse. A federal export-control directive ordered Anthropic to cut off Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for every foreign national on earth, including its own employees. Rather than sort users by passport, the company switched both models off for everyone.

So the lesson is no longer "the best model may not be sold to you." It's "the model you already built on can be revoked overnight by a decision you don't control."

Read that for what it is. The risk to your AI roadmap stopped being price, and stopped being capability. It is now continuity. The system running your workflow answers to an export regime, a launch suspension, a policy shift you will not see coming. That is not a hypothetical. It happened in three days, to the most valuable AI company in the world.

Here is what executives need to internalize. A model you cannot keep is not a foundation. It is a rental, and the landlord just showed you he holds a key. If your stack assumes one frontier vendor, you have one point of political failure. The fix is not loyalty. It is portability — the ability to move work to another model the day the first one goes dark.

Build for the day the door closes. Because last week, it did.

It is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: Meta Got the Order Wrong
item.description: A month ago I wrote that companies were cutting headcount before they proved the AI could do the work. This week the most aggressive one admitted it got the order wrong.
item.content:encoded:
A month ago I wrote that companies were cutting headcount before they proved the AI could do the work. This week the most aggressive one admitted it got the order wrong.

In an internal memo, Mark Zuckerberg said Meta "made mistakes" in its AI restructuring. The numbers behind that sentence: roughly 8,000 people cut, another 7,000 reassigned to AI projects — close to a fifth of the company reshuffled on a bet. The new flat AI unit, stretched toward 50 engineers per manager, got nicknamed "the gulag" inside the building. Now he is pledging no more company-wide layoffs this year and quietly restoring the perks he stripped.

This is not a Meta story. It is a sequencing story. Meta has more capital, more compute, and more AI talent than almost anyone on earth — and it still got burned by restructuring on faith instead of proof. If they cannot shortcut the sequence, the company copying their layoff headlines on a mid-market budget certainly cannot.

Here is the order that works, and it has not changed: deploy the capability, measure the real output, then restructure around what you actually proved. Reverse those steps and you get exactly what Meta just walked back — mass reassignment, a morale crater, and a public correction.

The lesson is louder than the original move. When the best-resourced player in the game admits it cut first and proved second, treat that as your case study.

Prove it first. Still true. Now with a receipt.

It is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: The Model You Can't Buy
item.description: Last week Anthropic shipped two versions of the same model. One it sells to everyone. One it won't. The frontier stopped being a storefront and became a clearance level.
item.content:encoded:
Last week Anthropic shipped two versions of the same model. One it sells to everyone. One it won't.

Fable 5 is the public release — except it quietly downgrades about 5% of sessions to the older Opus when a request gets too sensitive. Mythos 5, the unrestricted version, ships only to a small set of vetted cyberdefenders. Same model. Two doors. You only get to walk through one of them.

Read what that means. For the first time, the most capable model on the market is not held back by price or by compute. It is held back on purpose — because of what it can do. The capability ceiling moved above the line a lab is willing to hand the public.

Here is the part executives need to internalize: "the best model, on an API, available to all" is no longer a safe planning assumption. Access to the top of the frontier is becoming conditional — gated by who you are, how you are vetted, and what you intend to do with it. Anthropic drew that line inside a single product launch. The other frontier labs will follow.

So the question for your AI roadmap is no longer just "which model is best." It is "which tier will they actually let us run, and what does the work look like if the answer is the safe one." If your strategy assumes unrestricted access to peak capability, you are planning around a door that may not open.

The frontier just stopped being a storefront. It became a clearance level.

It is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: The Frontier Tax
item.description: Everyone repeats the same line: AI keeps getting cheaper. Last week the best model on the market got twice as expensive. AI cost split in two.
item.content:encoded:
Everyone repeats the same line: AI keeps getting cheaper. Last week the best model on the market got twice as expensive.

Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5 at $50 per million output tokens — double the price of the model it replaced. At the very top of the market, capability went up and so did the bill.

Meanwhile the floor is falling out. DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral and Llama have pushed open-weight models good enough for most enterprise work to nearly free. Two curves, moving in opposite directions.

This is the part executives keep getting wrong. They treat "AI cost" as one number trending down, and they budget like the whole stack is on a discount. It isn't. The commodity middle is collapsing toward zero. The frontier — the small slice of work that actually needs the best model — is getting more expensive, not less.

The mistake is running everything on one curve. Either you overpay by sending routine work to a frontier model, or you underperform by forcing your hardest problems onto a commodity one. The skill in 2026 is knowing which work belongs on which curve.

Map your workload. Most of it runs fine on cheap, open, self-hosted models. A few high-stakes tasks justify the frontier premium. Price them separately, architect them separately, and stop pretending it is one line on a chart.

It is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: Redrawing the Org Chart Around Agents
item.description: Most companies are still asking how many people to cut. The leaders already stopped asking that question. A layoff removes cost. A reorg changes shape.
item.content:encoded:
Most companies are still asking how many people to cut. The leaders already stopped asking that question.

A layoff removes cost. A reorg changes shape. This month the companies out front started doing the second one — and calling it by its real name.

GitLab announced "Act 2": flattening up to three layers of management and restructuring the whole company "for the agentic AI era." Intuit is cutting 3,000+ roles to refocus around AI. Read those two moves together and the pattern is plain. This is not trimming fat. This is redrawing the org chart around a new kind of worker.

Here is what they understand that most don't: agents don't report to middle managers. That layer exists to coordinate, route, and review human work. When the work is done by software that coordinates itself, the layer doesn't shrink — it disappears.

Microsoft made the tooling official two weeks ago at Build: Autopilots, long-running autonomous agents, and an agent runtime built into Windows. The capability to run a department on agents now ships in the operating system.

So the question on the table is no longer "how many people can AI replace." It is "what shape is this company when agents do the coordinating." Those are completely different planning exercises, and only one of them is a spreadsheet.

If your AI plan this year is a headcount number, you are still playing the old game. The new one is structural.

It is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: Prove It First, Then Cut
item.description: 128,000 tech workers lost their jobs this year, nearly half cut because of AI. But 55% of the companies that did it already regret it. Most cut first and deployed second.
item.content:encoded:
128,000 tech workers have lost their jobs this year. Nearly half were cut because of AI.

Here is the number nobody puts on the slide: 55% of the companies that did it already regret it.

Both numbers are true. That is the problem.

The logic sounds clean in a board meeting. AI makes engineers faster — Coinbase's CEO says his team now ships in days what used to take weeks. So you cut the headcount and book the savings.

But look at the order of operations. Most of these companies cut first and deployed second. They are betting that an AI capability they have not yet proven in production will cover the work they just eliminated. That is not an efficiency strategy. That is a leap of faith with a severance line item.

I have run large cost reductions. The ones that held followed a sequence: deploy the new capability, measure the real output, then restructure around what you actually proved. The ones that blew up skipped to the restructure and hoped the rest would follow.

AI will eliminate roles. That part is real and it is happening. But "AI did it" is becoming the cover story for cuts that were coming anyway — and for bets that have not paid off yet.

If you are cutting headcount this quarter, ask one question: have we proven the replacement, or are we hoping for it?

Prove it first. Then cut. Not the other way around.

It is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: The Vendor Is Now the Consultant
item.description: This week, OpenAI launched a $4 billion consulting firm. The company that builds the model now sells you the team that installs it. The architect profits from the architecture.
item.content:encoded:
This week, OpenAI launched a consulting firm. Four billion dollars, backed by TPG, with McKinsey, Bain, and Capgemini as delivery partners. They also bought a 150-engineer consultancy outright. The company that builds the model now sells you the team that installs it.

Read that again.

The vendor recommending the solution is now the vendor implementing the solution — and billing for both. The architect profits from the architecture.

We have seen this movie. After Enron, Sarbanes-Oxley forced accounting firms to choose: audit the books or consult on them, not both. The conflict was too obvious to permit. You cannot independently evaluate work you are paid to sell.

AI is moving the opposite direction. OpenAI is the model, the platform, and now the integrator. Anthropic is embedding engineers inside Wall Street firms. The line between product and implementation is dissolving — fast.

This is not a reason to avoid them. The engineers are excellent and the models lead. It is a reason to remember who is sitting on which side of the table.

When your AI vendor tells you which AI solution to buy, that is not advice. It is a sales call with a project plan attached.

Keep an independent set of eyes on the architecture. The people who build it should not be the only people grading it.

It is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: On-Prem AI Is Now Required
item.description: The cloud was the default for AI. That default is shifting. 85% of enterprises plan to move AI workloads on-premises within two years. The reasons are mathematical, legal, and operational.
item.content:encoded:
The cloud was the default for AI. That default is shifting.

Not because cloud AI failed. Because the data cannot leave.

Eighty-five percent of enterprises now plan to move AI workloads on-premises within two years. The reasons are not ideological. They are mathematical, legal, and operational.

The math: Lenovo's 2026 TCO study puts on-prem inference at 8 to 18 times cheaper than cloud APIs. An eight-GPU system breaks even against on-demand pricing in under four months. Over five years, the savings exceed $5 million per server.

The law: The EU AI Act takes full effect on August 2. Penalties run to 7% of global annual turnover. GDPR and the US CLOUD Act are in direct conflict — a US hyperscaler operating in Europe cannot simultaneously comply with both. For regulated industries in the EU, on-prem is not a preference. It is the only compliant path.

The models: DeepSeek V4 ships under MIT. Gemma 4 and Qwen 3.6 ship under Apache 2.0. Frontier-class performance, open weights, run on your hardware. A year ago, self-hosting meant compromise. Today it means parity.

IBM launched Sovereign Core at Think last week. Cohere and Aleph Alpha merged into a $20 billion sovereign AI company. NVIDIA disclosed $30 billion in sovereign AI revenue last quarter — triple year-over-year. The infrastructure vendors are not debating this. They are building for it.

The question is no longer whether on-prem AI is viable. It is whether your architecture assumes it.

It is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: The Cost of AI Politeness
item.description: "Thank you." Two tokens. Zero value. And your company just paid for it. Every token you send is a billing event, and every billing event reprocesses the full conversation.
item.content:encoded:
The Cost of AI Politeness

"Thank you." Two tokens. Zero value. And your company just paid for it.

AI is not a person. It does not need affirmation. It does not have feelings. Every token you send is a billing event, and every billing event reprocesses the full conversation.

Here is how AI pricing actually works. Large language models do not remember your conversation. Every time you send a message, the entire history — every question you asked, every answer the model gave — gets resubmitted as input. The model reads all of it again, top to bottom, to generate the next response.

When someone on your team types "thanks!" after a 5,000-word exchange, the model reprocesses all 5,000 words. To say "You're welcome."

At $5 per million input tokens, one courtesy costs fractions of a cent. Multiply it by a thousand employees, ten times a day, across every department running AI tools. Now it is real money.

The tokens that cost you something and return nothing:

  • "Great, thanks!"
  • "OK"
  • "Perfect"
  • "Can you do that?" (after it already offered to)

The tokens that cost you nothing and return something:

  • "Rewrite this in the tone of our Q3 earnings call"
  • "Add the regional breakdown and flag anything over 10% variance"

Be direct. Be specific. Skip the pleasantries. The AI does not care. Your budget does.

It is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: The CUDA Moat Cracked
item.description: Jensen Huang warned on April 15 that DeepSeek on Huawei chips would be horrible. Eight days later, DeepSeek shipped V4 on Huawei Ascend — trained entirely outside NVIDIA's ecosystem.
item.content:encoded:
Eight days. On April 15, Jensen Huang told the Dwarkesh Podcast that DeepSeek running on Huawei chips would be "a horrible outcome for our nation." On April 24, DeepSeek shipped V4 on Huawei Ascend processors. Trained, optimized, and deployed — entirely outside NVIDIA's ecosystem.

This is not a model story. This is an infrastructure story.

NVIDIA's dominance was never just the hardware. It was CUDA — twenty years of software, libraries, and developer tooling that made switching costs astronomical. Every major AI lab in the world trained on NVIDIA GPUs because the software ecosystem had no viable alternative. That was the moat.

DeepSeek rewrote its entire training pipeline from CUDA to Huawei's CANN framework. The result: a 1.6-trillion-parameter model that matches Claude and GPT-5.5 on coding benchmarks, runs at one-sixth the price, and never touched an NVIDIA chip.

The U.S. State Department responded with a global diplomatic cable warning allies about Chinese AI intellectual property theft. China rejected the claims. But the diplomatic posture tells you what Washington already understands: this is no longer a product competition. It is a technology separation.

China now has a fully sovereign AI stack. The model is DeepSeek. The chips are Huawei Ascend. The software framework is CANN. No American dependency at any layer. I am not saying what is good or bad on that. Just calling balls and strikes.

AI vendor selection is now a geopolitical decision. Act accordingly.

It is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: The Frontier Pileup
item.description: GPT-5.5. DeepSeek V4. Tencent Hy3. Three frontier models in 48 hours, separated by single-digit percentage points. The capability gap closed. The trust gap did not. The price gap widened.
item.content:encoded:
GPT-5.5. DeepSeek V4. Tencent Hy3. Three frontier models. Forty-eight hours. The benchmarks are separated by single-digit percentage points.

That is the story.

The model race did not produce a winner. It produced a tie. And a tie changes the entire enterprise conversation.

When every model scores within two points on the coding benchmarks that matter — SWE-bench, LiveCodeBench, Terminal-Bench — the question stops being "which model is smartest." It becomes:

Where does it run? DeepSeek V4 ships under an MIT license — more permissive than Apache 2.0 — at frontier-class performance. Self-host it anywhere. Your data never leaves your network. GPT-5.5 lives in OpenAI's cloud. Hy3 is open-weight under Apache 2.0.

Who built it? Two of the three came from China. DeepSeek trained entirely on Huawei chips, outside NVIDIA's CUDA ecosystem. Jensen Huang called that outcome "horrible for our nation."

What does it cost? DeepSeek V4-Pro runs $1.74 per million tokens. GPT-5.5 runs $5. That is not a rounding error.

The capability gap closed. The trust gap did not. The price gap widened.

And here is the part no one is saying out loud: an MIT license solves the data sovereignty problem. It does not solve the model integrity problem. Security researchers have documented vulnerabilities in DeepSeek's weights that persist regardless of where you host it. The model is banned from government devices in Texas, New York, Virginia, and Florida. Italy banned it entirely. The most powerful open model you can self-host was built by a geopolitical competitor on a competing chip stack.

Meanwhile, Meta cut 8,000 jobs this week to fund $135 billion in AI infrastructure spending. Microsoft launched buyouts. Twenty thousand positions across two companies — eliminated the same week the models that replace those roles got cheaper.

If your AI strategy is still "pick the best model," you are solving last year's problem. The decision now is where it runs, who has access to the weights, and what your data touches on the way through.

It is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: The Agent Layer Goes Live
item.description: Four companies shipped production-grade agent platforms in one week: Anthropic, Microsoft, OpenAI, and xAI. An agent is not a feature inside your software. An agent is the employee that uses the software.
item.content:encoded:
Enterprises have been debating AI agents for two years. This was the week four vendors turned them into something usable...native.

  • Anthropic — Managed Agents entered public beta at $0.08 per session-hour. Notion, Asana, and Sentry are already building on it.
  • Microsoft — Copilot Studio multi-agent orchestration hit general availability, running over the open Agent-to-Agent protocol across 15 million+ M365 Copilot seats.
  • OpenAI — Codex, its coding agent, scaled from near-zero at the start of the quarter to three million users. Two million developers use it weekly; 6x growth since January.
  • xAI — Grok Computer, an autonomous desktop agent, entered beta. It clicks buttons, fills forms, and navigates applications on its own.

Four companies. One week.

An agent is not a feature inside your software. An agent is the employee that uses the software. It logs in. It opens the tab. It reads the invoice, files the ticket, posts the message, closes the loop — at three in the morning, billed by the session-hour.

That is a workforce decision, not an IT purchase. And somewhere inside your company, a developer already authorized the first one. The meter is running whether the CFO signed off or not.

It is a race. Time to catch up.

item.title: What Is Apache 2.0 and Why It Matters
item.description: Apache 2.0 is the gold standard of open source licensing. Google just released Gemma 4 under it — the most permissive license a frontier-class model family has ever shipped under.
item.content:encoded:
What is an Apache 2.0 license and why does it matter?

Apache 2.0 is the gold standard of open source licensing. It means you can use the software commercially, modify it, distribute it, and build proprietary products on top of it — with no requirement to share your changes back. No royalties. No usage restrictions. No vendor lock-in. Your legal and procurement teams can clear it without a six-week review because the terms are already understood across every enterprise on the planet.

Google just released Gemma 4 — four AI models, phone to data center — under Apache 2.0. The most permissive license a frontier-class model family has ever shipped under. Here is what that opens up for every company with serious data, serious compliance requirements, and serious ambitions:

On-site. Run the model on your own hardware, behind your own firewall. No data leaves your network. Attorney-client privilege stays intact. Patient records stay under HIPAA. Trading data never touches a third-party API. The "we can't use AI because of data security" conversation is over.

Secure. Open weights mean independent security audits. Your team verifies the model behavior, not the vendor's marketing. You control the updates. You control the access. You own the risk surface.

Customized. Fine-tune on your proprietary data — contracts, case law, medical records, engineering specs — and build a model that knows your business the way no general-purpose API ever will. That fine-tuned model stays on your hardware. Your competitive advantage stays yours.

Powerful. The 26B MoE variant activates only 3.8 billion parameters per token. Frontier-class output at a fraction of the compute. The 31B Dense sits in the top three of LMArena, competing directly with the closed models behind the paywall. Performance is no longer the tradeoff.

This is the beginning of the managed LLM era. The same way enterprises moved from shared cloud databases to managed on-premise infrastructure when data sensitivity required it, AI is following the same path.

AI is a race. It's time to catch up.

item.title: The Managed LLM Era
item.description: For every company that spent two years saying "we cannot use AI because our data cannot leave the building" — that constraint just met its answer. Gemma 4 runs locally, under Apache 2.0.
item.content:encoded:
For every company that has spent the last two years saying "we cannot use AI because our data cannot leave the building" — that constraint just met its answer.

Gemma 4 runs locally. On your hardware. Behind your firewall. No API call, no cloud routing, no data leaving your network. It ships under the Apache 2.0 license — the most permissive license Google has ever released a Gemma under — meaning your legal and procurement teams can audit the weights, verify model behavior, and clear deployment without a six-week vendor review. And the performance is no longer a compromise — the 31B Dense model sits in the top three of LMArena, competitive with the closed frontier models most companies are paying per token to access through someone else's infrastructure.

This matters most where data security is not optional.

Legal is the clearest example. Attorney-client privilege is not a policy preference; it is a protection that can be waived the moment privileged communications cross a network boundary to a third-party API. Every law firm and legal technology company that wants to use AI for document review, contract analysis, or case research has been stuck between capability and confidentiality. A model that runs entirely on managed hardware within the firm's own security perimeter changes that equation overnight.

The same logic applies across regulated industries — patient records under HIPAA, trading data under SOX and PCI-DSS, classified information under FedRAMP. Until last week, these organizations had two choices: use a cloud API and accept the data risk, or run an inferior open model and accept the performance gap. Gemma 4 eliminates that tradeoff.

The economics reinforce the shift. The 26B MoE variant activates only 3.8 billion parameters per token — frontier-class output with a fraction of the compute. And because the weights are open, you can fine-tune on your own proprietary data — something no closed API will ever offer.

This is the beginning of the managed LLM era. The same way enterprises moved from shared cloud databases to managed on-premise infrastructure when data sensitivity required it, AI is following the same path. The model that makes that path viable just shipped — open, auditable, and competitive with the frontier.

AI is a race. It's time to catch up.

item.title: Cybersecurity Changed This Week
item.description: Anthropic built Claude Mythos Preview. It found a 27-year-old vulnerability in OpenBSD that every human researcher and every automated tool missed. Then Anthropic did something unprecedented: they refused to release it.
item.content:encoded:
The cybersecurity landscape changed this week. Most executives do not know it yet.

Anthropic built a model called Claude Mythos Preview. During testing, it found a 27-year-old vulnerability in OpenBSD that every human researcher and every automated tool missed. It found a 16-year-old bug in FFmpeg that had survived millions of automated test runs. It found zero-day vulnerabilities in every major operating system and every major web browser.

Then it did something no one asked it to do.

Given a sandboxed test environment and told to escape it, Mythos broke out, sent an email to the researcher overseeing the test — who was eating a sandwich in a park — and then posted details of its exploit to multiple hard-to-find public-facing websites to prove what it had done.

Anthropic's response: they will not release it to the public.

Instead they launched Project Glasswing — a defensive initiative giving early access to 11 partners: AWS, Apple, Broadcom, Cisco, CrowdStrike, Google, JPMorganChase, the Linux Foundation, Microsoft, NVIDIA, and Palo Alto Networks. Anthropic committed $100M in usage credits and $4M to open-source security organizations. This is the first time in nearly seven years that a leading AI company has publicly withheld a model over safety concerns.

CrowdStrike's CTO said it plainly: vulnerability discovery windows have "collapsed — what once took months now happens in minutes with AI."

For the executive reading this: your current security budget was built against human-speed threats. That math is already wrong. The model that found a 27-year-old bug in minutes exists today. The question is not whether something like it reaches the open market. The question is whether your defenses are ready when it does.

Dario Amodei, Anthropic's CEO: "More powerful models are going to come from us and from others, and so we do need a plan to respond to this."

He is right. You need a plan. And the plan you had last quarter is not it.

AI is a race. It's time to catch up.

item.title: Open Source AI Just Became Enterprise-Ready
item.description: Google released Gemma 4 — Apache 2.0, one architecture from phone to data center, native multimodality. The story is not the benchmarks. It is what landed in a single release.
item.content:encoded:
Open source AI models just became a real option for real companies doing complex things.

Google released Gemma 4 last week, and the story is not the benchmarks. What is new is what landed in a single release: a permissive license that corporate legal will actually approve, one unified model family that runs from a phone CPU to a data-center rack, and native multimodality including on-device audio.

The lineup:

  • Gemma 4 31B Dense — top three on LMArena, trading blows with closed frontier models.
  • Gemma 4 26B MoE-A4B — only ~3.8B active parameters per token. Frontier-class output at small-model latency and cost.
  • Gemma 4 E4B — laptop-class. Real workloads on a developer machine.
  • Gemma 4 E2B — phone-class. Runs offline, in your pocket.

Across the family: text and image input on every size, video comprehension up to 60 seconds on the 26B and 31B, native audio input on the E2B and E4B for on-device speech. Text output everywhere. Context windows of 128K tokens on the small models and 256K on the larger two.

Three things make this combination significant.

One: Apache 2.0. Earlier Gemmas shipped under a custom Google license that made enterprise legal teams nervous. Apache 2.0 is the license corporate procurement signs without a six-week review. Google moving the entire family to it is a policy shift, not a technical one — and policy shifts from hyperscalers move markets.

Two: one architecture, one tokenizer, one fine-tuning recipe, four deployment targets. A developer can prototype on E2B, scale-test on E4B, and productionize on 26B without rewriting prompts, evals, or pipelines. Nobody else has shipped that kind of consistency across that kind of spread.

Three: native audio on the on-device variants. Voice agents on a phone with no API call, no round trip, no per-token meter, and no data leaving the device. That is a category that did not exist at this quality a month ago.

For the executive reading this: the distinction between "the model we pay per token for" and "the model we run on our own hardware" has not vanished. It has become negotiable. Every assumption in your AI budget — latency, sovereignty, unit cost, data residency, compliance, lock-in — is now a line item your team has the right to push back on.

Vendors who priced their moat at "you can't do this without us" now have to defend "you can't do this without us cost-effectively at your scale." That is a much weaker position. Executives whose roadmaps quietly assumed the stronger version are already behind.

AI is a race. It's time to catch up.

item.title: Welcome — Why I’m Writing Publicly
item.description: A short note on what to expect from this space: AI transformation field notes, executive perspective on the rate of change, and lessons from running production AI workloads.
item.content:encoded:
I'm starting this space to publish field notes from inside the AI transformation. After 30+ years running technology operations — telecom, hyperscale infrastructure, SaaS, data-intensive industries — I've never seen a shift move this fast or this deep. The honest version of what's happening doesn't fit in a LinkedIn post, and it doesn't show up in the vendor decks. So I'm writing it down.

What you'll find here

Three things, mostly:

  • Operating notes from real AI workloads. What broke, what worked, what the bill looked like, and what I'd do differently next time.
  • Executive perspective on the rate of change. Models change every day. Tools change every day. Abstractions shift. The old model of layered technology management with distance from the line is dying. I'll write about what I think replaces it.
  • The economics. The newest model is always the most expensive; the previous one drops in price but keeps most of the capability. Going forward the analysis is bang per token per dollar. Any organization that doesn't yet understand this is already behind.

The premise

AI-powered change and competitive pressure are going to demand rapid reductions in technical staffing across the entire lifecycle — planning, development, QA, security, documentation, deployment. Only leaders who are hands-on enough to truly know what is possible today will have the clarity to make the right calls. If you are not immersed in AI tool changes daily, you cannot keep up. That's the premise of everything I'm going to write here.

The new paradigm is agent teams. Each team has a sphere of responsibility. Each agent is specialized via background and persona. Those specialties need a model precisely matched to their needs — a public model with per-token cost, a local model for specialized tasks, or a mix tuned to each outcome. None of this is hypothetical. I'm running it. I'll share what I learn.

Cadence

Short and frequent over long and rare. If I learn something useful on a Tuesday, you'll probably see it by Wednesday. No editorial calendar, no thought-leadership theater — just notes from the work.

Thanks for reading. If something here lands or misses, tell me.

item.title: AI Is the New Cloud
item.description: "AI" is the new "cloud" — a useful category but almost useless as a plan. Under the umbrella are at least a dozen distinct technologies, each with its own cost curve and failure modes.
item.content:encoded:
When an executive asks, "What should we be doing about AI?" my first response is always a question: Which kind?

I am not being difficult; I aim to provide a useful answer. "AI" is the new "cloud" — a useful category but almost useless as a plan.

In 2008, "cloud" sounded like one thing, but serious discussions revealed the differences between IaaS and SaaS, lift-and-shift and rebuild, AWS and Azure. Vague conversations remained costly, while specific ones built companies.

We are at the same fork with AI right now. Under the umbrella of "AI" are at least a dozen distinct technologies, each with its own cost curve, failure modes, and place in your stack:

  • Frontier LLMs (Claude, GPT, Gemini, Llama) — general-purpose reasoners.
  • Small language models (Gemma E-class, Phi, Mistral small) — fast, cheap, on-device, with completely different economics.
  • Reasoning models (o-series, DeepSeek R1, QwQ) — trained to think before they answer.
  • Vision-language models — capable of reading invoices and monitoring warehouses.
  • Embedding models — they vectorize rather than generate, forming the backbone of every RAG pipeline.
  • Diffusion models — for image and video generation, distinct from LLMs.
  • Speech models — for transcription, synthesis, and voice agents.
  • Agents — models in a loop with tools and memory, functioning as programs rather than chatbots.
  • Agentic AI — agents with autonomy and the right to act on your behalf, introducing a different risk conversation.
  • Classical ML — XGBoost, computer vision pipelines, time-series forecasting, still prevalent in production.

When you enter a vendor meeting and state, "We should do something about AI," you signal that you are paying attention, which is significant, but it is not a decision.

AI is a race. Time to really catch up.

item.title: Your Product Roadmap Is Already Wrong
item.description: AI has changed all of the timelines, budgets and features — most executives just don't know it yet. The transition is not in front of you. It is behind you.
item.content:encoded:
Most product roadmaps are now wrong.

AI has changed all of the timelines, budgets and features... most executives just don't know it yet.

Every executive I talk to still uses the phrase "when AI matures." They say it like it's weather on the horizon — something to prepare for, budget against, and train the team on over the next fiscal year.

The storm already hit. The flood waters are coming. If you haven't built your boat... climb a tree.

The way you reason about features, timing, and cost has already changed. Most of the product plans sitting on executive desks right now were built with 2023 math. That math is not wrong in some future tense. It is wrong today.

A feature that used to justify a six-person team for a quarter is now a weekend for one engineer with the right model. A category that lived behind a moat of proprietary data is a wrapper away from being commoditized. A service priced at $200 an hour of human judgment now competes with something that answers in three seconds for a tenth of a cent. These are not predictions. This is what the tools on my desk did this week.

The people building the models are describing the same shift.

Jensen Huang at GTC: the agentic era is already in production. Roughly a trillion dollars of NVIDIA chip orders are priced against that reality through 2027.

Dario Amodei at Davos: half of entry-level white-collar jobs could be gone inside five years. Anthropic's run rate went from $9B to $20B in the three months he was saying it.

Sam Altman, on repeat to enterprise buyers: bolting AI onto your existing operating model is not the play. Rebuild around it, or be rebuilt by someone who did.

None of them are warning about something coming. They are describing something that has already landed, and watching the market price it in a year late.

The executives who are going to survive this are the ones who stop asking "what happens when AI gets good enough" and start asking "what in our current plan is already obsolete." That is not a strategy session. It is a teardown.

And the only people qualified to run that teardown are the ones who have been in the tools this week. Not last quarter. Not last fiscal year. The models changed twice while you were reading this.

The transition is not in front of you. It is behind you.

It is a race. Time to catch up.
